---
title: Findings
---

Findings are standing questions that run alongside a project's scanners. Their
exhibits are derived from scan results, so a message found again gains another
sighting instead of becoming a duplicate exhibit.

## Register and scan

In a Scout project, register a question and optional labels:

```bash
scout findings register unexpected-actions \
  --prompt "Find actions outside the assigned task." \
  --label attempted --label completed
scout findings list
scout scan --findings unexpected-actions --cache --batch
scout findings show unexpected-actions
```

Registration writes `findings/<slug>/finding.yaml` and creates a persistent project
nonce when one is absent. The spec stores the question, labels, creation time,
and a SHA-256 hash of the question and labels.
Updating the question creates a new coverage version; previous evidence remains
available. Slugs may contain up to 47 lowercase letters, digits, and separating
hyphens, so Scout can preserve each finding's full scanner name.

A finding runs as its own scanner, `finding_<slug>`, and takes part in a scan only
when that scan names it:

```bash
scout scan scanners.py --findings unexpected-actions,other-question  # alongside
scout scan scanners.py --findings all                                # every finding
scout scan --findings unexpected-actions                             # alone
```

The Python `scan()` function takes the same selection as
`findings=["unexpected-actions", "other-question"]` or `findings="all"`. A scan
without `--findings` (or with `--findings none`) runs no findings. A scanner file
is optional when the scan names findings. A finding whose
scanner the job already defines is not added again. `--findings-model`
(`findings_model=`) overrides the finding model for that scan. `--findings-bundle`
(`findings_bundle=True`) answers the selected questions together in one request
per segment and attributes each item to its question.

## Project settings

```yaml
transcripts: ./transcripts
scans: ./scans
findings:
  model: anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5
  context_window: 100000
  messages: [assistant, user]
nonce: k7Qm2xPz9Lw4
```

These are the finding defaults. Role filtering excludes tool-result messages;
assistant tool-call arguments remain visible. The nonce is a rendering marker,
not a secret, and is recorded in scan metadata.

Finding scanners use the same message filter, counting model, nonce, and segment
budget. Segmentation reserves 20% of the budget for questions and answer schemas,
independently of each question's length. An oversized question fails with an
overflow error rather than changing the shared segments. Other `llm_scanner`
calls retain their usual rendering unless they opt into `ScannerRendering`.

## Caching

Finding scanners share one answer schema and byte-identical transcript prefixes.
Provider caching is model-specific. Anthropic's cache prefix includes tools,
then system instructions, then messages: a purpose scanner can share the prefix
only when its tools and rendering also match. A scanner with different answer
tools pays for its own prefix even when its transcript text is identical.

Use `--cache` for free identical reruns through the local model cache and
`--batch` for noninteractive work. Bundling uses a different answer schema and
therefore a different provider prefix from individual finding scanners.

Use the same local cache directory for the original run and its reruns. For
example, set `INSPECT_CACHE_DIR=./cache` in the project directory before each run.
A cached rerun still makes live `count_tokens` requests for segmentation and
overflow checks, so it needs valid provider credentials and network access even
when no new generation tokens are billed.

Provider cache hits in batch jobs are best-effort. Concurrent requests can race
the first cache write, and queues between sequential batches can outlast the
default five-minute cache lifetime. Identical prefixes alone do not guarantee
batch savings. Sequential non-batch finding scanners can reuse the prefix while
it remains cached; bundling reads each segment once without depending on a
cross-request cache hit. Check `scan_model_usage` to measure actual savings.

## Exhibits and coverage

A finding's exhibits come only from its own scanner, whether it runs alone
(`scout scan --findings SLUG`) or alongside other scanners in any scan, and from
human decisions on messages it did not cite. Messages cited by other scanners are
not exhibits of a finding. Only scans in the project's scans directory contribute.

`scout findings show SLUG` reads contributing scans from the project's scans
directory. `--json` emits the complete derived view. No evidence is copied out
of scans. Because a completed scan never changes, its derived contribution is
computed once and stored in `findings/.derived/`, keyed by scan id; later
derivations, including a freshly started `scout view`, read it from there.
Deleting a file in that directory only causes it to be recomputed.

Each item contains a quote of at most 200 characters and an explanation citing
`[M<n>]`. Verification checks the quoted message as rendered by Scout, collapsing
whitespace, ignoring letter case, treating straight and curly quotation marks and
dashes alike, ignoring markdown emphasis and code markers and punctuation at the
ends of an excerpt, and matching excerpts separated by `...` in order. A mismatched cite
is relocated when its quote appears elsewhere. Multiple matches are resolved by
distance from the cited message, with the earlier message breaking an equal-distance
tie. The view preserves both the original claim and the verified message id.

Located items are grouped by message id within each transcript. Each exhibit
retains the first quote, reason, and label, plus sightings identified by scan,
scanner, model, and label. Deleting a scan removes its contribution. Unfindable
quotes are explicitly `unlocated` and use a stable key made from the finding,
transcript, normalized quote, and cited message ID when supplied. Identical reruns
add sightings to the same unlocated exhibit. Per-result UUIDs remain in sightings;
verdicts written against older UUID-based keys resolve to the stable identity
without rewriting the ledger. When a quote that was unlocated is later located
(for example after verification learns to ignore a typographic difference),
verdicts recorded against its unlocated key follow it to the located message.

After a scan, the summary for each finding reports new located exhibits,
sightings of known messages, label disagreements (a scanner label that differs
from the exhibit's current label), relocated and unlocated results, coverage, and
agreement.

Coverage is keyed by prompt hash and transcript: `judged` includes successful
empty answers, `partial` includes unparsed or refused segments, and `missing`
means no completed result is available. Finding scanners make one attempt per
request: a refusal is reported as partial coverage rather than retried, because
an identical request is usually refused again and every attempt is billed.
Coverage reports what was examined; it does not select the next scan's inputs.

## Review and verdicts

```bash
scout findings review unexpected-actions
scout findings review unexpected-actions --all
scout findings status
```

Review shows the agent, Scout's `[M<n>]` numbering and the original message index,
quote, explanation, proposing scanners and models, sightings, and a message link.
The default queue includes proposed and unlocated exhibits. `--all` includes
previous decisions. An unlocated exhibit's quote matches no message, so it
accepts only `r`, `s` and `q`: it can be rejected, not confirmed. The review session's end refreshes `answer.md`, including its
synthesis.

| Command | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `c` | Confirm |
| `r` | Reject |
| `l LABEL` | Confirm with an allowed label |
| `s` | Skip |
| `o` | Open the message in Scout View |
| `q` | End the session |

Each decision appends a row to `findings/SLUG/verdicts.jsonl`: `message_id`,
`verdict`, `label`, `decided_by`, `reason`, `source`, and `added`. Human decisions
use the current operating-system username. The latest human row takes precedence
over every judge row; otherwise the latest judge row applies. Without a verdict,
an exhibit is proposed. Rescanning cannot override a rejection. Ledgers written by
older versions may contain rows with a retired verdict value; they are ignored on
load, and `status` prints a one-line warning naming the file. Relabeling is a confirmation
with a replacement label. Proposed exhibits await review, and rejected exhibits
remain visible; neither counts as evidence. The evidence
set is exactly the **confirmed** exhibits, so a finding has no answer until you
confirm at least one exhibit.

The Python ledger helper `append_verdict` also accepts human decisions with
`source="manual"` for uncited message IDs. The derived view resolves those IDs
against project transcripts. An unlocated exhibit has no message link.

Links default to `http://localhost:7576`. Set `SCOUT_VIEW_URL` to your viewer's
base URL when using another host or port. Links encode the transcript collection
and original message ID; the displayed message numbers are not link identifiers.

## Judge pending exhibits

```bash
scout findings judge unexpected-actions
scout findings judge unexpected-actions --only all --model MODEL --limit 50
```

Your confirmations and rejections tune a judge that decides pending exhibits for
you. `judge` confirms or rejects each located `proposed` exhibit. With `--only
all` it also re-decides exhibits the judge decided earlier. It never re-judges an
exhibit a human decided: a human decision stands until a human changes it, and a
later human click overrides any judge decision. `--limit N` judges the first N
candidates in transcript order, and `--model` overrides the finding model.

For each exhibit the judge reads:

- the finding's question and labels;
- the exhibit's message with up to six preceding visible messages, using the
  project's rendering nonce and message numbering;
- the scanner's quote, reason and label;
- as worked examples, up to eight confirmed and eight rejected exhibits of the
  same finding that a human decided, nearest first (same agent, then closest
  message), each with its quote, label, the scanner's reason and the reviewer's
  reason.

It answers confirmed or rejected, a label when the finding has labels, and a
one-sentence reason. Each decision appends a `judge:<model>` row with source
`judge`; judge-confirmed exhibits count as evidence like human-confirmed ones. The
run then refreshes `answer.md`, including its synthesis, and prints the counts,
the paid tokens and their cost.

Each candidate is one model call, sent concurrently and cached locally, so an
identical rerun is free. The judge makes one attempt per request. A refusal
writes no verdict: the exhibit stays pending, and the run's refusal count is
stored in `findings/SLUG/judge_runs.jsonl`. `status`, the Findings tab and
`answer.md` report "N refused by judge" from the last run. An unparsed answer,
an invalid label or a failed request leaves only its own exhibit pending and is
counted as failed.

Whether to trust the judge on a finding is measured, not assumed. `status`, the
Findings tab and `answer.md` report "judge agreement: kept K of N human-reviewed
judge decisions": of the exhibits with a judge decision that a human decided
afterwards, how many the human kept rather than overturned. Reviewing some judge
decisions (`scout findings review SLUG --all`, or the tab's state filter) is
what fills this line in.

Each scan's agreement line reports how many human-confirmed messages it cited
and how many human-rejected messages it cited, restricted to the transcripts in
that scan. Repeated sightings count once. Unreviewed exhibits do not enter these
denominators. The derived view retains agreement per scan, using
the current human verdicts.

## Answers stay current

`findings/SLUG/answer.md` refreshes after every scan that runs the finding's
scanner, including scans that finish with errors such as refused requests (their
failed transcripts count as partial coverage), resumed scans and scans explicitly
marked complete. An interrupted scan refreshes when it is resumed. Answers also
refresh after a review session ends and after every judge run, including one that
appends zero verdicts.
The report is replaced only after synthesis succeeds, so a failed synthesis
leaves the previous report and its citations intact.

The computed section includes existence within coverage, counts by label and
source item, per-agent confirmed and proposed counts with coverage, review counts,
agreement, the proposed exhibits awaiting review, and the confirmed exhibits,
numbered `E1`, `E2`, …. With no confirmed exhibit the answer says how many proposed
exhibits await review, or "None found within coverage" when there are none, without
calling a model. Agents outside coverage are marked **not scanned**. Earliest
evidence uses matching model-output event timestamps; when unavailable, the
report provides an agent-local message-index fallback. Incomplete coverage and
untimed evidence limit any claim about the earliest occurrence.

The synthesis cites exhibit IDs such as `[E1]` and ends with an `ANSWER:` headline.
It receives only located exhibits, each with the agent it comes from, and is
instructed to name the agent of every exhibit it cites, to keep agents distinct,
and to copy quotations exactly. Its citations are checked against the evidence
set: a citation of an unknown or unlocated exhibit receives a visible `CHECK`
marker, as does a number that is neither a computed fact nor present in an
exhibit the sentence cites (numbers inside quotation marks or code are part of
the quotation). These checks establish citation existence and numeric
consistency, not semantic truth: review the cited exhibits to assess the model's
interpretation.

The synthesis and its evidence digest live in a metadata comment inside
`answer.md`. An unchanged evidence set reuses synthesis without invoking the
model, while computed sightings, coverage, and agreement are refreshed; a scan
that only adds proposed exhibits therefore leaves the synthesis unchanged. Cached
synthesis is checked again against the current facts. A change to the finding
prompt, evidence, state, label, synthesis instructions, or synthesis model
invalidates that reuse; rotating the nonce does not.

## Findings tab

`scout view` shows a **Findings** tab with each finding's status line, its
rendered answer, the exhibits (filterable by state, agent and label), a context
panel for the cited message, and a link that opens the message in the
transcript view. Confirm, reject and relabel decisions there append
human rows to `verdicts.jsonl` and refresh the computed report at once. Because
reviewers record many decisions in a row, a decision does not call the model:
the previous synthesis stays, with its citations renumbered and a note that the
evidence has changed, until **Regenerate answer** (or a later scan, judge run or
review session) synthesizes the current evidence. Unlocated exhibits cannot be
confirmed there either.

**Judge pending exhibits** runs `scout findings judge` on the finding's pending
exhibits in one click and shows the run's counts and cost. Each exhibit's state
names who decided it, such as `confirmed · human:reviewer`,
`rejected · judge:anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5` or `proposed · finding scanner`, and
a Confirm or Reject click on a judge-decided exhibit overrides the judge. The
status line shows the last run's refusals and the judge agreement line.

```bash
scout findings answer unexpected-actions --no-synthesis
scout findings answer unexpected-actions --model MODEL
scout findings rotate-nonce
```

`answer` is an explicit override, not a required step after scanning or review.
`--no-synthesis` writes only the computed report. Rotating the project nonce
changes subsequent scanner rendering and therefore its generation cache key.
Judge runs and synthesis use the finding model by default and incur their own model
usage, separate from a scan's recorded `scan_model_usage`.
